title: Two die in Leeds car crash after police pursuit
description: Two people have been killed after their car was hit by a vehicle fleeing from police in Leeds.West Yorkshire Police said it happened at 00:44 GMT, whe
body: Two people have been killed after their car was hit by a vehicle fleeing from police in Leeds.West Yorkshire Police said it happened at 00:44 GMT, when a blue BMW 123D failed to stop for officers in Gelderd Road and then crashed into a white Volkswagen Scirocco.The driver of the Volkswagen, a 22-year-old man, died at the scene. His passenger, a woman, 23, died later in hospital. Both were from York.The occupants of the BMW, a 39-year-old man from Harrogate, two boys aged 16 and 17 and a 16-year-old girl, have been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.The 39-year-old is also being held on suspicion of driving while over the prescribed limit for cannabis, the force confirmed.The teenagers in the BMW were taken to hospital for treatment to injuries that were not considered life-threatening.A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said a referral had been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which confirmed it had started an investigation.

schema.headline: Two die in Leeds car crash after police pursuit

title: Three men sentenced to death in Jordan over church mass shooting
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Nine people were killed in the shooting at the Greek Orthodox church last monthByElla KiplingA Jordanian court has
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Nine people were killed in the shooting at the Greek Orthodox church last monthByElla KiplingA Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out a fatal mass shooting on a church last month.The attack on 23 October killed nine people and injured 34 others who had been attending a Christian funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts". The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified.Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud.Figure caption, Watch: CCTV footage appears to show gunmen near churchA second video showed dead and wounded people lying on the ground amid chaotic scenes at the church.It is still unclear why the attackers chose to target that specific church.Shortly after the attack, Jordan's King Abdullah II wrote on X: "The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. "Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity."The three men fled the scene of the shooting and were later located inside an abandoned house in Karak governorate, south of the capital, Amman.They refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and wounded all three of them, the Public Security Directorate said at the time. No security personnel were hurt in the shootout.King Abdullah praised security forces for chasing the suspects "to the very end".The week after the Karak shooting, Jordan struck what its military said were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation to the church attack.Syrian health officials told state media that five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province. Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists" without giving further details.Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government, but Syria said it had not been notified in advance.Executions in Jordan are carried out by hanging. The kingdom previously observed an unofficial ban on executions from 2006 to 2014, and another pause from 2017 until June this year.

schema.headline: Three men sentenced to death in Jordan over church mass shooting

title: Man dies after being hit by ambulance on A19 near Sunderland
description: A man has died after being struck by an ambulance transporting a patient near Sunderland, police have said.Northumbria Police said the crash occurred
body: A man has died after being struck by an ambulance transporting a patient near Sunderland, police have said.Northumbria Police said the crash occurred on the A19, between the junctions for the A1018 and A690, shortly after 02:00 GMT.The ambulance was travelling on the northbound carriageway and did not have its blue lights on when it hit the man, who was in his 30s and died at the scene.Neither the patient nor their partner who were travelling in the ambulance were injured in the collision, while the vehicle's driver, a man in his 40s, was also not hurt and remained at the scene to assist police with their inquiries.The North East Ambulance Service (NEAS) said the patient in the ambulance and their partner were transferred to another ambulance.Officers from Northumbria Police's roads unit have launched an investigation into the collision.Sgt Ben Rutherford said: "Our thoughts are firmly with the family and loved ones of the man who has tragically died following this collision."We will continue to support them in any way that we can at this incredibly difficult time."Anyone with CCTV or dashcam footage of the incident itself or the moments leading up to the collision has been urged to contact the force.Rutherford said anyone with information, no matter how insignificant it may seem, "could prove key to our investigation and help provide answers for the man's loved ones".

schema.headline: Man dies after being hit by ambulance on A19 near Sunderland

title: England team news: Thomas Tuchel omits Jarrad Branthwaite, James Garner and Josh King for Spain game
description: England manager Thomas Tuchel has omitted Josh King, James Garner and Jarrad Branthwaite from his squad to face world champions Spain in Madrid on Sun
body: England manager Thomas Tuchel has omitted Josh King, James Garner and Jarrad Branthwaite from his squad to face world champions Spain in Madrid on Sunday night.England travelled to Spain with a squad of 26 players but Uefa rules state that only 23 players can be selected in a matchday squad for Nations League gamesThe return to fitness of Ezri Konsa and Djed Spence - who missed Thursday's win over Croatia - has been a contributing factor in the trio's omission.Arsenal defender Konsa could come straight back into the starting XI while James Trafford will replace Jordan Pickford in goal.Garner replaced Declan Rice in the 77th minute of the 2-1 victory over Croatia at Wembley, scoring a goal that was subsequently disallowed, while Everton team-mate Branthwaite and Fulham's King were unused substitutes.King received his first senior call-up for the two final Nations League fixtures in Group A3, but the midfielder, 19, will not feature in this international window.However, fellow first-time call-ups Jobe Bellingham and James Hill are included.Arsenal defender Ben White, who was booed when he came on as a substitute against Croatia, is also part of the reduced 23-man party.England sit three points behind Spain in their group and know that a win will secure top spot in the table, as they already have a superior goal difference to their opponents.Tuchel's side are already guaranteed a quarter-final spot and a first-place finish will secure them a tie against one of the runners-ups in one of the three other groups in League A.The two-legged quarter-finals will be played in March, with semi-finals and a final to be played in June.In the build-up to Sunday's fixture, Tuchel reminded his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocols, with the match to be the national team's first in the Spanish capital since a notorious game at Real Madrid's Bernabeu stadium in 2004 which was overshadowed by racist chanting aimed at England players.The Spanish federation was fined last month and ordered to play their next friendly match with a partial stadium closure after fans sang "Islamophobic and xenophobic" chants about Muslims during a game against Egypt."We had the same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September 2025]," Tuchel said. "There is a protocol in place."Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid]."The England coach's comments were dismissed by Spain coach Luis de la Fuente, who said: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism."Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."

schema.headline: England team news: Thomas Tuchel omits Jarrad Branthwaite, James Garner and Josh King for Spain game

title: Ebola in DR Congo: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola.
description: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can surviveImage source, Braton Serge/BBCByRuth AlongaBBC AfricaReporti
body: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can surviveImage source, Braton Serge/BBCByRuth AlongaBBC AfricaReporting fromButemboWhen Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there."Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience."As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.Image source, Braton Serge/BBCImage caption, Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga uses his book to help convince sceptics that Ebola is realThe first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre."She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.Image caption, Dr Kamwanga's mother says his experience has helped dispel some of the misinformation she had heard about EbolaThe current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment."The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified."I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged."We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns."We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola. Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust."I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact." During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says."Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing."The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease."Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."More from the BBC on the Ebola crisis:

title: The lessons in handshaking and eye contact preparing pupils for the world of work
description: Schools and colleges across England are legally required to have a careers programme, including expanded opportunities for work experience, and to use
body: Schools and colleges across England are legally required to have a careers programme, including expanded opportunities for work experience, and to use the updated Gatsby Benchmarks, external to structure their careers education.The Gatsby Foundation's Beth Jones, who developed the guidance, says the more careers education benchmarks a school achieves, the less likely it is their students will leave as Neet."Careers guidance cannot solve every barrier young people face, but it is an important part of helping them navigate their futures successfully," she says. There is no doubt that improving careers education and giving pupils more vocational options is part of the plan for schools, but it is not the whole picture for solving the Neet crisis. As Milburn himself pointed out in his interim report, external earlier this year, from the moment a child arrives at school at age four, the system can predict "who is most likely to fail".A child starting school without basic "school-ready" skills like potty training at ages four or five is nearly three times as likely to be Neet by the time they reach 16 or 17 years old.Pupils with special educational needs, from poorer backgrounds, or those with mental health issues are also more likely to be Neet. The problem might not be identifying the pupils that need help, but finding the funding to help them. The Institute for Fiscal Studies warned that a "one-size-fits-all approach" to the Neet crisis was "unlikely to work, given the very different circumstances of young people who are Neet".It says a "key question for the government will be how much they are willing to invest in the short run in the hope of a pay-off in future years".

schema.headline: The lessons in handshaking and eye contact preparing pupils for the world of work

title: Sandpaper scandal: Bowler Chadd Sayers says he took sandpaper from the field and rejects Pat Cummins recount
description: Former Australia bowler Chadd Sayers says he helped take sandpaper off the ground in the match before the infamous Cape Town Test and has backed Usman
body: Former Australia bowler Chadd Sayers says he helped take sandpaper off the ground in the match before the infamous Cape Town Test and has backed Usman Khawaja's recollection over Pat Cummins' - saying he believes "everyone knew" about the plan to ball tamper.Sayers, 39, was 12th man during the second Test of the 2018 series against South Africa in Gqeberha, previously known as Port Elizabeth, and backed the claim from Khawaja's book that sandpaper was also used there."It was given to me to take off," Sayers said on SEN Radio."That wasn't planned or anything. It was a wicket or drinks break after tea."Sayers also said there was a "60 to 90-minute" meeting in the Australia dressing room after Bancroft had been caught using sandpaper in Cape Town, in which players discussed taking collective responsibility - something Khawaja claims but Cummins said he did not remember in his extraordinary news conference on Friday."I am comfortable sitting here that I believe everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used," said Sayers, whose one Test was the final match of that series."It [sandpaper] was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in the changing rooms."I'm not taking sides, it's just my recollection of what took place."After the occurrence in Cape Town, we all sat in the changing rooms after that day's play and, probably for 60 to 90 minutes, we talked about what had happened and I guess where to next."

schema.headline: Sandpaper scandal: Bowler Chadd Sayers says he took sandpaper from the field and rejects Pat Cummins recount

title: Woodbridge lorry driver, 91, knits 200 hats
description: A 91-year-old man has proven it is never too late to learn a new skill after taking up knitting and making around 200 hats, including for babies in ho
body: A 91-year-old man has proven it is never too late to learn a new skill after taking up knitting and making around 200 hats, including for babies in hospital.Stanley Workman, from Woodbridge in Suffolk, took up the craft five years ago when his late wife, Jennifer, was gifted knitting looms but showed little interest in them.What started out as a humble hobby to pass the time turned into a passion project, with the former lorry driver handing them out free of charge.Many of his head-warming creations have been donated to the St Mary's Shop, which sells products to raise money for St Mary's church in the town.He joked that he had made one of the hats for himself but "I don't know what I've done with it".Workman, who has lived in Woodbridge since being moved from Bristol to the town when he was fostered as a young boy, has been a supporter of the church for years.The father-of-three, who drove lorries for a garden centre for 48 years, also served as the church's warden from 2012 to 2018.

title: ‘I get emotional thinking I’ll be off the streets by Christmas’
description: Image caption, Dexter and his dog Reginald have been offered a bed as part of the scheme to get rough sleepers off the streets before ChristmasByHanna
body: Image caption, Dexter and his dog Reginald have been offered a bed as part of the scheme to get rough sleepers off the streets before ChristmasByHannah MillerPolitics Reporter, BBC Bristol and Pete SimsonPolitics producerWork has begun to try to meet the prime minister’s pledge to offer all rough sleepers a route off the streets before Christmas.Andy Burnham made the promise on his first day in the job and the government has since allocated more than £12m to the West of England Combined Authority to tackle homelessness over the next three years.In Bristol, the number of people sleeping rough has increased steadily since Covid, with the council's monthly street count now approaching the highest-ever recorded.One charity said it was "confident" accommodation could be found for everyone currently in need but that long-term success would depend on making sure the right support and housing was available."They actually came to me today and said they're going to house me from three o'clock this afternoon,” Dexter, who has been sleeping rough for 18 months, said.He said he was delighted to have somewhere to go."More than anything it's really, really boring,” he said. “The worst bit of it is people just walk by. You're kind of invisible a lot of the time. "Them coming and offering me housing today was quite a surprise. It came out of nowhere."Dexter said he had not previously asked for help because he had not wanted to be separated from his dog, Reginald.He has been told, though, that there was now space for them both."I'm pretty chuffed with that because I can't cope without this one [Reginald]," he explained. "He keeps me sane on a day-to-day basis, gets me up in the morning."Dexter said he became homeless as a result of experiencing depression and alcoholism after losing a close friend."There's been a lot of times where I've felt incredibly vulnerable," he said."I don't think I'll find myself out here again. I want to get back towards doing some work."Image caption, Patrick has been in a shelter before and said he found it difficult but that he wanted to try againPatrick said he had been homeless on-and-off for eight years, since a family breakdown."I lost my family and my job in one fell swoop," he said. "It sent me a bit depressed, I couldn't cope on my own."My self-esteem went down and I just haven't been able to get back on my feet."He said his most recent shelter placement lasted about two months, ending after he had friends over when overnight guests were not allowed."They gave me all these rules but they didn't help me to cope with being lonely indoors,” he said.Patrick admits that the prospect of being responsible for bills was also daunting but he said with the right support he thinks he could succeed. He said being off the streets by Christmas would mean "happiness, security" to him."I get emotional thinking about it," he said. "A future - it would mean a lot."I hope they're not lying. I would really like to be housed."‘Big logistical challenge'St Mungos delivers homeless outreach services on behalf of the city council.David Ingerslev, from the charity, said: "I am confident we'll have an offer for everyone.”He said the charity was trying to set up a range of options to meet different people's needs in different locations across the city."There are women-only spaces, spaces where pets can be accepted, places with different amounts of support of available," he said. But Ingerslev said it was "a really big logistical challenge" to have the right places available for the right people at the right time.He estimated there would need to be about 200 extra bed spaces in the city to meet demand."We're preparing for all eventualities," he said."Some people won't accept the offers and where they don't we're going to put additional support in place for people affected by things like mental health issues, learning difficulties, or substance misuse.”'Attractive city'Ingerslev said one of the biggest challenges was finding something more permanent for people placed in an emergency shelter.Supported accommodation is often the best option but all 900 of the city’s beds are currently taken."The move-on from [supported housing] is much slower than it used to be,” Ingerslev said. "We need to unlock the supported accommodation that we have."However, that requires affordable housing for people to move into and Ingerslev said high housing costs in the city were at the root of the problem because they increase demand for social housing and make it harder to buy potential supported accommodation properties."It's an attractive city to come and live in,” he said "but that's contributing to the pressure on the housing market."If you see someone sleeping rough, you can contact StreetLink, external to connect them to support.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: ‘I get emotional thinking I’ll be off the streets by Christmas’

title: Holly Humberstone on her identity crisis - and struggle being compared to other pop stars
description: Holly Humberstone: People can't connect to a pop star who's 'too polished'Image source, Silken WeinbergImage caption, Holly Humberstone says she was h
body: Holly Humberstone: People can't connect to a pop star who's 'too polished'Image source, Silken WeinbergImage caption, Holly Humberstone says she was having an identity crisis on a weekly basisByMusic correspondentYou might know her as a pop star, endorsed by everyone from Taylor Swift to Sam Fender, but Holly Humberstone has a secret double life. In her spare time, the singer-songwriter is literally a cat burglar."We've stolen one of our neighbours' cats by accident," she laughs, in a Zoom call from her fixer-upper in New Cross, south-east London. "He's a tiny little black cat who's come into our garden and simply chosen us."Under the slightest scrutiny, however, her story crumbles like a biscuit in a hot cup of tea."OK, we've been coercing him into the house with treats," she admits. "He's just so cute."But we're not trying to keep him. We literally push him out every night."Humberstone's excuse for this feline felony is that, last year, her parents sold her childhood home in Lincolnshire, external and moved to Wales  – taking her pets with them.One, a cat called Tsuki, had even been immortalised in the song Lucy as a confidante who listens to her problems but "never judges"."Oh, she knows some secrets!" laughs the singer. "I'm so glad she can't talk.""We actually tried to bring her to London with us, but she's a countryside cat and she hated it so much. We had to send her to Wales where she can be free and frolic."Her parents' relocation was disruptive for the human Humberstones, too. Their house, a "freezing cold, falling down" property 20 minutes outside of Grantham, played a huge part in the singer's success.Her early EPs were all written there, inspiring the "wonky sonics" of her indie-leaning pop sound. The 2021 single Haunted House is even dedicated to the "friendly" spirits who inhabited the property."It's a place I always felt I could go back to, to remind myself of who I am," she says. Instead, she spent 2025 "packing up 23 years of stuff my family and I had accumulated", from her old ballet shoes and poetry books to forgotten bits of jewellery.Image source, Holly HumberstoneImage caption, The singer shared photos of her old bedroom, and the artefacts she'd rediscovered, while clearing out her parents' "haunted house" in Grantham (pictured, left).The process was unsettling. Already grappling with the idea of leaving childhood behind, Humberstone found herself literally throwing away her past."I felt uprooted. I was having some sort of identity crisis almost weekly," she says.So she did what she's always done, and poured those feelings into her second album, Cruel World, which entered the UK charts at number four earlier this year."Writing these songs felt like building myself a little shield and a kind of safety bubble," she says. "There's an escapist, fantasy element to so much of the album."Maybe that's true, but Humberstone has always had the ability to locate a song's emotional core, and the lyrics on Cruel World don't disappoint."To lose somebody is to know you're only human, honey," she sings on To Love Somebody, external, soothing her elder sister as she endures an agonising break-up.Undeterred by that heartbreak, she throws herself headfirst into a new affair on Die Happy, external, declaring: "Hit the gas, I want it fast, want it reckless."But the most revealing song is the closing track, Beauty Pageant, external.Fragile and raw, it's the sound of Humberstone in her dressing room, addressing the woman in the mirror who'd "die for the applause" but who struggles with the impossible beauty standards imposed on female artists.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Humberstone's biggest songs include Falling Asleep At The Wheel, The Walls Are Way Too Thin, Die Happy and Scarlett"That's a song that I wasn't really setting out to write," she confesses."Writing about other people often feels easier than turning the magnifying glass on yourself."The lyrics, she says, draw on a "very specific" mindset she acquired at her all-girls school in Grantham."It was drilled into me: You're all in competition. You're only rewarded if you're the best. And if you're not, you're worthless."The experience "really warped the way I view other girls", she says.Musical success made it worse. After winning the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, Humberstone found herself competing with megastars, even though her music leaned towards the alternative side of pop."I'm a very small fish and I recognise that, but suddenly I was in meetings being compared to all these people on my label's roster, who are on a completely different scale," she says."It's something I really, really struggled with in the early days and it's something I've really had to unlearn."Nowadays, Humberstone has stopped benchmarking herself against her peers, recognising that the need for validation never fades."I don't think that there's a point I could get to, or an award that I could win, where these feelings would disappear," she says."Everybody feels like they've still got something to prove, so I'm done with setting myself goals - because then I lose sight of the real reason that I'm doing this, which is to write music that represents me, and have other people feel understood through that music."Image source, Silken WeinbergImage caption, "I pray that one day I'll turn and face the mirror with a smile," sings Humberstone That mindset comes to fruition in the new, expanded edition of Cruel World, whose five new songs were largely written after the original album was handed in."I was super proud of Cruel World and, when you've got that in your back pocket, there's room to experiment and break some of your usual parameters."The new tracks find Humberstone embracing a new persona – more confident, more flirtatious, a little salty – with music inspired by a playlist featuring Abba, Madonna and Robyn.The single Too Cute To Be Lonely, external is a will-they/won't-they story set at a house party."Don't leave a girl upset, in such a pretty dress," she teases the object of her affections.Terminally Yours takes place a couple of weeks later, when Humberstone realises she's fallen head-over-heels in love."Your stupid face is my sorry fate," she harrumphs, cross at herself.  "For [expletive]'s sake, I'm in love."Silver Sky, a gorgeous acoustic ballad, tells another side of the story, as she settles into her lover's arms and drifts into blissful reverie."I wrote that on a kind of Hail Mary trip, seeing what fell out of the air in Nashville," she reveals."We went over to [co-writer Maddie Diaz's] house, took a guitar into the garden and wrote Silver Sky outside, while all of these gorgeous red cardinals were singing around us."I usually write a lot about my mental health struggles, but I was just in the mood to write something that made me feel good."Image source, JME InternationalImage caption, Humberstone won the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, joining the ranks of former winners such as Sam Fender, Florence + The Machine and AdeleNot that her mental health issues are in the rear view mirror. Humberstone admits her stage nerves have only intensified since the release of Cruel World."It's the proudest I've been of any of my work and, for that reason, I struggled with shows because I felt a lot of pressure to go out and deliver it to the standard that I think people are expecting."But on the other hand, it's totally fine if you mess up or sing a wrong note. People can't connect to a pop star that feels too robotic and polished. "So maybe my strength is that vulnerability, and I need to recognise that more."That vulnerability has won Humberstone millions of fans, even if a hit single has (so far) eluded her. And her audience keeps growing.  In May this year, her breakout single Falling Asleep At The Wheel was awarded a silver disc... five years after its release, indicating that her songs have staying power in an era of disposable hits.Astonishingly, this is news to Humberstone, who learns about the accolade during our interview. But it helps to clarify a thought that's been knocking around her head."If I'm going to be doing this for years to come, I've just got to keep making music that feels right, trusting my gut and realising there's no end point," she says."Reaching an end point would mean I've 'made it', but I think, maybe, that's a myth that doesn't really exist."

schema.headline: Holly Humberstone on her identity crisis - and struggle being compared to other pop stars

title: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds - but are they value for money?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByLucy HookerDaniel Thomas and Faarea MasudBBC business reportersIt's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Li
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByLucy HookerDaniel Thomas and Faarea MasudBBC business reportersIt's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach."I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering.Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar.Image source, Getty Images/SkimsImage caption, Customers likened the contents of Kim Kardashian's Skims calendar to something you would find down the back of a sofaThis week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa.Julia says she earns a good salary but is keen to get value for money and doesn't want to waste it on items she won't use."I spent £160 on a Space NK fragrance calendar last year," she says. "I got some fragrances I'd been wanting for a while for a lot less than recommended retail price, and those I didn't like I managed to sell on for a slight mark-up on what I paid."Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Julia, 39, says she thinks fragrance calendars are usually good value for money  Beauty calendars, which often cost upwards of £100 and sometimes much more, have been around for more than a decade and the marketing has grown ever more sophisticated.High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight. And it appears to be working. Ipsos data shows, external around 15% of all advent calendars sold are beauty ones, with people aged 18-34 particularly willing to splash out.But in the face of that tsunami of marketing, customers seem to be getting savvier."I love beauty, but I rarely buy beauty advent calendars. They are pricey and often only have a few things that I actually want to try or are trending products," says Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist.She thinks some are good value but, for her, the advantage is being able to try on a small scale without forking out for a full-size product."For me, an advent calendar - particularly a beauty one - serves the purpose of allowing me to try out different products, particularly in the lead-up to Christmas, and then I can hopefully snag a bargain in the Boxing Day sales."Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist, says the calendars "serve the purpose of allowing me to try out different products"Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, also likes the general idea, but has a healthy scepticism around a lot of them in practice. "I do think some brands take the consumer for granted in that they provide each day with something so menial that people are bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items. "And when that's the case, they certainly put me off as the excitement to open each window dwindles into irritation rather than joy."Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, is less keen on the calendars and says they leave consumers "bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items"Jessica Jasper, a marketing consultant, is more positive - she thinks it's worth it. But she also thinks some companies are just jumping on a trend and that "some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing".So can beauty calendars offer value for both the brands and the customer - an example of a win-win? Or are they mainly designed to make us spend more at Christmas than we need to?Image source, SuppliedImage caption, "Some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing," says marketing consultant Jessica JasperHeather Widdows, a philosophy professor and beauty expert, has pointed out that while you might buy some of the products in an advent calendar individually, it's highly unlikely you'd buy all of them.  "Beauty calendars may offer you lots of products for a really good price. They can also be a bit of fun and feel sensuous. "But it is exceptionally unlikely that you would use all the products inside them, so they're probably not worth it." This year, Julia has spent £99 on a John Lewis fragrance calendar which she thinks is good value for money. But it doesn't mean she'll keep everything in it.In fact she's joined a Facebook group where people trade the ones they don't want for ones they do. "The ones I keep are already a lot cheaper per mililitre than if you bought them at retail," she says.With additional reporting from Kris BramwellGet in touchHave you bought something you didn’t feel was value for money? Or seen misleading discounts on products?

schema.headline: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds - but are they value for money?

title: Schoolboy imposter subjected former professor and wife to 'terrifying ordeal'
description: Image source, AlamyImage caption, Brian MacKinnon lived a double life as teenage student Brandon LeeAn imposter who made headlines around the world fo
body: Image source, AlamyImage caption, Brian MacKinnon lived a double life as teenage student Brandon LeeAn imposter who made headlines around the world for posing as a school pupil in his 30s has appeared in court and admitted hiding in the home of his former university professor before subjecting him to a "terrifying ordeal"Brian MacKinnon targeted Prof Brian Whiting, 87, as he lay in bed with his wife, the day after a BBC docudrama on his ruse was broadcast.My Old School chronicled MacKinnon's return to Bearsden Academy, as Brandon Lee, a 16-year-old who had supposedly just moved to Scotland from Canada.MacKinnon hatched the plan so he could pursue his dream of becoming a doctor having been thrown out of Glasgow University, when Prof Whiting was dean of the medical school.MacKinnon - who was formerly a pupil at the East Dunbartonshire school from 1974 to 1980 - returned in 1993 and secured five As in his Higher exams.As a result he earned a place at the University of Dundee to study medicine.But in 1995 an anonymous tip-off revealed he had previously spent two years as a medical student at the University of Glasgow and did not complete the course.MacKinnon was thrown out of the medical school in 1983 following a failed appeal.When his double life was exposed, Prof Whiting was interviewed by BBC Scotland News.The archive footage was used in the 2022 docudrama, which starred Alan Cumming as MacKinnon.Details of the case, which called before the High Court in Glasgow on Thursday, were first reported in the Mail on Sunday, external.The court heard MacKinnon, now 63, went to the retired academic's home on 28 September last year - the day after My Old School had been repeated on the BBC.Figure caption, Prof Brian Whiting speaks about Brian MacKinnon in a BBC interview from September, 1995It is believed MacKinnon sneaked into the property, in the west end of the city, around 16:30 as the rear door and gate were unlocked.Prof Whiting was in his study and his 83-year-old wife, Marlene, was in the garden.They went to bed around 23:30, unaware MacKinnon was hiding in their home.About two hours later they were awoken when their room door suddenly opened.A figure wearing dark clothes, a grey cap and a mask over the lower part of his face walked up to the side of the bed and told Marlene: "No lights."Prosecutor Eilidh Robertson told the High Court in Glasgow: "She sat up and MacKinnon demanded that she lie back down or he would really hurt her."Both the Whitings were very frightened by this point. "MacKinnon then pointed at her husband and asked: 'Is that Brian Whiting?'."MacKinnon then said he had brought "two statements" which he wanted the couple to "release".Robertson said MacKinnon threatened to kill the couple and hurt their families if they did not comply.Image caption, Alan Cumming played MacKinnon in the 2022 film, My Old SchoolMarlene did not know who the intruder was before he said his name was "Brian MacKinnon".Robertson added: "MacKinnon then spoke to Brian Whiting directly blaming him and two colleagues for ruining his life and having responsibility for the death of his parents."MacKinnon then briefly left the room and, on his return, suddenly asked to be let out the house.Marlene got up and led him downstairs hoping he would go.She asked how he had initially got in, he boasted: "That was easy."Marlene got a good look at MacKinnon after he took off his mask.The advocate depute said: "She unlocked the front door. "As MacKinnon was leaving, he stated that he had people working for him that would check if the witnesses were complying with his demands."If not, they would be dead. He then left the house and turned down a lane."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, MacKinnon returned to Bearsden Academy in 1993, having previously left in 1980 Marlene immediately called her son. He went on to show her an online photo of MacKinnon and she identified him as the man who had invaded their home.The court heard how the two statements left by MacKinnon had been made to look as if they had been completed by Prof Whiting.Each alleged the retired dean had "succumbed to intolerable pressure to make a misleading statement about Brian Lachlan MacKinnon".They also said: "Via a BBC Scotland television broadcast, I stated falsely that MacKinnon had not met the required standard as a medical student after he had set out to study medicine at Glasgow in 1980. Nothing could have been further from the truth."The documents claimed there had been a "conspiracy" to exclude "incandescently bright" students like MacKinnon.Image source, AlamyImage caption, Pupils at Bearsden Academy reading the revelations about the ex-pupil Brandon LeeThey also included "defamatory" remarks about Glasgow University, BBC Scotland and Alan Cumming.MacKinnon was not initially traced but DNA recovered at the house helped link him to the crime.CCTV from a nearby property had also captured him walking near the Whitings property that afternoon.MacKinnon was eventually arrested as he returned to his home in Milngavie, East Dunbartonshire, hours after the incident.Police Scotland officers went on to recover a mobile phone and three notepads.In one, there was handwritten text which stated: "I will regain a place to study medicine at a reputable university".An envelope was also seized and a "statement" similar to those given to the Whitings was discovered inside.MacKinnon made no comment when quizzed by detectives.Image caption, MacKinnon appeared in stage production of South Pacific while at high schoolLast week he was brought into court in a wheelchair and pleaded guilty to a charge of attempted extortion. Sean Templeton, defending, told the hearing: "It is clear that he has had an extraordinary life, thrust into the public gaze in the 1990s by attending a school when he was over the age of 18."He added MacKinnon had always wanted to be involved in medicine to "assist the public", but his "ambitions to become a doctor came to an end".Templeton said after he was exposed, it had "characterised" his life in the many years since, including the docudrama which MacKinnon "did not agree to".The defence advocate said: "It is something that has dogged him since the 1990s."MacKinnon had been assessed by a psychiatrist after his initial appearance in court in late September last year, but it was eventually concluded that he was "fit to stand trial".Templeton told the court MacKinnon was "frail" and suffered from uncontrolled movements in one of his arms.Lady Anwar continued his remand in custody as sentencing was deferred for reports until a later date. MacKinnon is currently being held at HMP Barlinnie in Glasgow. She told him: "You subjected Mr and Mrs Whiting, both in their 80s, to a shocking and terrifying ordeal in their home. "It is likely you will face a significant custodial sentence."

schema.headline: Schoolboy imposter subjected former professor and wife to 'terrifying ordeal'

title: Australia vs England: Tom Banton, Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker impress as tourists level series
description: Second one-day international, AdelaideEngland 355-6 (50 overs): Banton 121, Cox 67, Root 62Australia 220 all out (44.3 overs): Green 64, Renshaw 63; A
body: Second one-day international, AdelaideEngland 355-6 (50 overs): Banton 121, Cox 67, Root 62Australia 220 all out (44.3 overs): Green 64, Renshaw 63; Atkinson 4-28England won by 135 runs; series level at 1-1ScorecardTom Banton scored a century and Sonny Baker and Gus Atkinson impressed with the ball as England's wildly inconsistent one-day team hammered Australia to set up a series decider.Banton scored a fine 121 – pushing his case for selection further with a second ODI hundred – in England's 355-6.After being knocked over for 131 two days ago in Perth, England's total was their highest in one-day internationals in Australia.And then their bowlers, who failed to defend 430 against Sri Lanka last month and were undone by an improbable last-wicket partnership against Pakistan, reduced Australia to 29-4 inside seven overs and easily closed out a 135-run victory.The win ends a seven-match losing run against Australia across formats in Adelaide - and a run of six consecutive defeats by Australia in 50-over cricket away from home.But, more significantly, it corrects their course after those damaging defeats against Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Australia and offers positives amid the frustrations going into the decider on Wednesday (03:30 GMT) in Hobart.Will the real England please stand up? Before those defeats in Rawalpindi, Lahore and Perth, England had won three ODI series this year.This win only adds to the feeling they are extremely difficult to figure out.Banton was superb and, even more encouragingly, Atkinson and Baker were too.This England team has often struggled for new-ball wickets and Baker, brought in for Jamie Overton in an attempt to correct that fault, found significant swing. He took the key wicket of Australia captain Mitchell Marsh, taken high at slip by a diving Joe Root, for two.Atkinson used nip to nick off Travis Head for seven – the second match in a row he has dismissed the Australia left-hander – and also have both Cooper Connolly and Josh Inglis caught behind. Career-best figures of 4-28 are reward for good recent performance that have often gone unrewarded.England were not perfect. They dropped four catches – first Inglis and then Matt Renshaw and Cameron Green, who made 63 and 64 respectively to drag out Australia's score.But by the end, Sam Curran had taken two wickets in two balls, including bowling Jack Edwards with his moon ball, in a boost after his poor run. Green was also out stumped when the ball deflected off Jordan Cox's shin and onto the stumps and Liam Dawson took 2-41 as he was preferred again to Adil Rashid.These are the performances that suggest England can challenge at next year's World Cup, but plenty more are needed.Cox came in after captain Harry Brook, on five, deflected the ball onto his stumps when trying a ramp to push on the scoring. Jacks joined him when Banton holed out at deep square-leg after one too many of those pulls.Cox and Jacks were scoring at a run a ball when taking England to 245-4 after 40 overs but together helped their side take 110 from the last.Cox, after a run of lower scores as he fills in for Jos Buttler, drove, cut, scooped and pulled. A reverse scoop for four off Xavier Bartlett was outrageous. He has one more chance in this series to push his case further - possibly more if Buttler does not recovery for the January series against South Africa."Banton has really found his flow for batting," former England captain Michael Vaughan said."I don't know who the person was to say 'you can open the batting in 50-over cricket, Tom' but it's been a tremendous move. He and Ben Duckett look a good combo."Banton seems to have all the time, all the strokes. He's got the pull shot, he's got the drive down the ground and he plays spin great. He hasn't looked like he's trying to hard to score runs, he's just batted."

schema.headline: Australia vs England: Tom Banton, Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker impress as tourists level series

title: Onions in your socks? Why homespun cold remedies work for some
description: Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Deborah Powis says putting her feet in a bag of chopped onion helps reduce her coughByJo MakelEast Yorkshire and
body: Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Deborah Powis says putting her feet in a bag of chopped onion helps reduce her coughByJo MakelEast Yorkshire and LincolnshireDeborah Powis has a trick she swears by when she gets a cough.I have stopped her on the street in the market town of Horncastle, Lincolnshire, to ask what cold remedies she turns to at this time of year."You chop up an onion," she begins. "You put it in plastic bags, put your feet inside and put your socks over the top."You do this overnight – yes your sheets smell in the morning, but you can wash your sheets."The 62-year-old midday school supervisor says her daughter has also started using this method."I know it works. I don't know the science behind it, but it does stop the cough."It may sound like folklore, but as one expert explains, other homespun remedies have been tested in the lab and work – at least for some people.According to Prof Alyn Morice, head of respiratory medicine at the Hull York Medical School, genetics mean some remedies, such as menthol, work better within particular families."Sometimes a person can have a good response to menthol and other people don't. And it often runs in families," he explains.And how our brain and nervous system responds to treatment can also make a difference – even to a placebo.Image source, University of HullImage caption, Prof Alyn Morice recommends honey and lemon for a coughMorice runs the Hull Cough Clinic, one of the largest centres in Europe, helping people with chronic coughs."Sore throat, you can have paracetamol for. But the cough can be really troublesome," he says."What I recommend in the first option is a dollop of honey in the bottom of a cup, then squeeze of lemon, pour in hot water and mix it all up. This does actually work."It coats the lining of the throat and decreases the amount of irritation of the receptors in there, which are giving you the tickle, which is making you cough."It's called the demulcent effect. And that's why most remedies that you can buy over the counter are syrups."According to the UK Flu Survey, external, 47 per cent of us take time off work or school with flu-like symptoms. Most of us treat ourselves at home, with the NHS recommending, external rest, plenty of fluids and taking paracetamol or ibuprofen to lower the temperature and treat aches and pains.Image caption, Aden Kelly says Jakemans makes about three million menthol lozenges a dayOne substance many of us have turned to is menthol, whether by dissolving crystals in a steamy bowl, rubbing ointment on our chest or sucking on cough sweets.Jakemans, in Boston, has been making what it calls "menthol confections" for almost 120 years.  As it is autumn, staff have been turning out about three million lozenges a day. Even outside the factory, there is a warming aroma of menthol and aniseed."It can help if you have a scratchy throat, it can help ease that. It has menthol in it, so can give you that lift which we all need." says sales director Aden Kelly."Are they a placebo? Or do they work?" I press."I certainly get a lot of relief," says Kelly. "I do a lot of talking in my job. So, I personally find they work very well."You might expect that answer from the sales director. But Morice says menthol has a proven effect."Menthol actually reduces the amount of coughing – I showed that many years ago," he says."So, you can either inhale menthol or you can have it in a cough lozenge, which decreases the amount of coughing."Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Jakemans, based near Boston,  has been making lozenges since 1907Back in Hull, the consumer health firm Reckitt produces well-known self-care treatments, including Lemsip.It contains paracetamol and a decongestant, phenylephrine. But home remedies have influenced the product."It was introduced back in the 1960s. It was a lemon-flavoured hot drink designed to relieve cold and flu symptoms," says Dr Mark Ripley, a senior vice-president for research and development."When people get sick, they'll have a warm cup of tea or cocoa. And the idea here was to combine that ritual of a warm beverage with real medicine."And of course, lemon, honey, ginger, blackcurrant – some of the flavours that we have – they're all associated often with home remedy."Family loreLike Powis with her onions, parents and grandparents pass down advice to the next generation.And as Morice explains, there is a genetic reason why certain treatments become family favourites."The thing with all these agents and remedies is that different individuals respond differently to them," he says."This tendency to cough and have relief of cough from certain remedies is inherited."So, if there's a family lore that says 'we use menthol and it works very well', then it's probable that children in the family will also respond to the same menthol lozenge or inhaler."So why do placebos also work for some people? "Normally, coughing is held with the brakes on by the brain," Morice says."In some people, if you stimulate these brakes, you reduce the coughing. It's not just them imagining it – it is a demonstrable, neurological nerve effect from the brain controlling the cough."So could this be why Deborah knows her onions work for her?Morice says it is possible there is "a germ of truth" in this remedy and that the smell has an impact."Perhaps they have found in her family, it alters their perception of the cough."Listen to highlights from Hull and East Yorkshire or Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North.Download the BBC News app from the App Store, external for iPhone and iPad or Google Play, external for Android devices

schema.headline: Onions in your socks? Why homespun cold remedies work for some

title: Hannah Fry feels 'unbelievably lucky' after cervical cancer treatment
description: Prof Hannah Fry has described feeling "unbelievably lucky" after being treated for cervical cancer. The mathematician and BBC presenter, who recently
body: Prof Hannah Fry has described feeling "unbelievably lucky" after being treated for cervical cancer. The mathematician and BBC presenter, who recently took part in the second season of the Celebrity Traitors, said cancerous cells were discovered after she attended a cervical screening in 2020.She underwent a hysterectomy, describing the experience to BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs as "horrific". "As awful as that was, it had a full stop at the end of the sentence," the 42-year-old added. "I had my five-year clear the other day. I feel so unbelievably lucky."In Sunday's episode, Fry told show host Lauren Laverne that she had delayed a cervical screening examination for months in 2020. After she attended one, the results "didn't come back for a few weeks," she said. "Then I got a call from my GP telling me they needed me to come back and do another test, and they did a biopsy."I was trying hard not to panic but when they found it was in the lymphatic system… that was when it really started to come down."The broadcaster said she was told that her chances of survival depended on the cancerous cells not having spread to her lymph nodes, although it was not clear "how bad it was at that point"."It's all about, basically, how far into your lymphatic system has it got. If it had not got into any lymph nodes, then the odds were in my favour and I had a really good chance of survival," she said.Fry explained that this meant "if it was in one it would drop to a 60% chance of survival and two – the odds would go against me and it would be a 40% chance".While in isolation in hospital following her hysterectomy, Fry said a surgeon told her that four of her lymph nodes had appeared enlarged.She added: "I was in this hospital bed on my own and no-one could come and visit me for over a week, with nothing but the sheer terrifying drop of the end of my existence in front of me – it was horrific."Fry described not being able to "think back to happy things that... have already happened because it is sad", while also not being able to "look forward to things you are hopeful about because it doesn't feel like it is there".She also said she asked her then husband to set up FaceTime in the corner of a room so she could watch their two young daughters play while she was in hospital."I didn't want them to see me, it was too much," she said.But she added: "Going through something like that I don't think I would swap it. "I think it was honestly such a gift to have that experience when you're 36 and then come out the other side of it."The presenter grew up in a working-class family and studied mathematics at University College London.She later completed a PhD in fluid dynamics, and last year became Cambridge University's first professor of the public understanding of mathematics.Fry has fronted BBC science series including The Future with Hannah Fry and The Secret Genius of Modern Life.She was banished in the latest series of The Celebrity Traitors after being exposed as a traitor.

schema.headline: Hannah Fry feels 'unbelievably lucky' after cervical cancer treatment
